items.q: Why do big goals fail even when motivation is high?
items.a: You **fall to the level of your systems**, not rise to your goals. A novel needs a writing habit; a marathon needs a training process. Without supporting systems, ambition collapses into comfort.

items.q: What is the plateau of latent potential?
items.a: The **invisible lag** between effort and visible results — the valley where most people quit. Compounding looks flat until it crosses a threshold; keep the system through the silent stretch.

items.q: How should you think about habit change if outcomes feel far away?
items.a: Every action is a **vote for the type of person** you want to become. Decide identity first, then prove it with **small wins** — you become a runner by running regularly, even a little.

items.q: What are Clear's four laws of behavior change?
items.a: Map the habit loop to design rules: make it **obvious**, **attractive**, **easy**, and **satisfying**. Invert all four to break bad habits.

items.q: Do disciplined people just have more willpower?
items.a: Often no — they are **better at avoiding temptation cues**. Redesign the environment so good habits are default and bad habits require friction.

items.q: What should you do before optimizing habits?
items.a: Run a **habit scorecard**: list daily habits and mark good / bad / neutral relative to who you want to become. You cannot change what you do not see.

items.q: How do implementation intentions and habit stacking differ?
items.a: Implementation intention fixes **time and place** (*I will [behavior] at [time] in [location]*). Habit stacking anchors to an existing routine (*After [current], I will [new]*).

items.q: How does the two-minute rule stop procrastination?
items.a: Scale the habit to a **gateway under two minutes** — open the book, put on shoes, write one line. Those minutes **are** the habit at first; motion beats planning-as-delay.

items.q: What is the cardinal rule of behavior change?
items.a: **What is immediately rewarded is repeated; what is immediately punished is avoided.** Add short-term satisfaction (tracking, small rewards) so long-term habits survive.

items.q: What should you do after you miss a day?
items.a: **Never miss twice.** One miss is an accident; two starts a new unwanted habit. Resume immediately, even with a tiny two-minute version.
